title: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Any system of particles that conserves quantities such as particle number and momentum and has sufficient microscopic randomness will show the same large-scale fluid behavior, so a discrete cellular automaton particle model can reproduce the flow of real fluids.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: so long as certain physical quantities such as particle number and momentum are conserved, then whenever there is sufficient microscopic randomness, it is almost inevitable that the same overall fluid behavior will be obtained.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fluid Flow” (from p. 376), p. 379. Scope: fluids and discrete lattice-gas models of fluids

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Hydrodynamic limits of specified lattice gases are amenable to simulation and, in some cases, proof, with extensive fluid benchmarks available. Interventions on conservation laws offer good discrimination. The any-system wording omits assumptions that cannot be exhausted empirically, so the broad claim is only partial.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Simulate particle systems that vary microscopic rules while preserving or breaking specified conservation laws and measure convergence of coarse-grained fields to hydrodynamic equations and benchmark flows. Conservation-preserving randomized systems that systematically fail to show fluid behavior would refute sufficiency.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Universality is asymptotic and finite-size effects can be large.

Sufficient microscopic randomness and same overall behavior require thresholds.

Additional symmetries and locality assumptions may be necessary.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mass and momentum conservation plus molecular chaos is the standard route to the Navier-Stokes equations, and lattice-gas rules can be rerun and compared with public turbulence fields. Breaking a conservation law changes the large-scale equation, which is a clean control. For ordinary fluids the claim can be confirmed or refuted with existing theory and data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Derive or simulate the large-scale momentum equation for particle or lattice-gas rules that conserve mass and momentum, and compare the resulting flow, at matched Reynolds number, with laboratory or direct numerical solutions of ordinary fluids. Universal Navier-Stokes behavior when the conservation laws and a randomness condition hold, and a different large-scale law when they are broken, would support the claim; a conserved, sufficiently random particle system whose large-scale flow is not hydrodynamic would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Complex fluids are outside the ordinary fluids the claim is aimed at.

The hydrodynamic limit assumes enough randomness and isotropy; some conserving rules stay correlated and do not yield simple viscosity.

discriminating power: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.7
